hook: A student guesses on a 10-question quiz and gets 3 right. Which 3? It could be the first three, the last three, or any of many other sets. To find how likely 3 right answers is, you first need to count how many different sets of 3 questions there are. Factorials and combinations do that counting without listing every case.

prereq.q: A count X can be 0 to 10. Which values are "at least 9"?

figure.caption: All six teams of 2 from 4 people. A team is a set, so order does not matter: ${}_4C_2 = 6$.

chain.effect: there are n choices for the first place, n − 1 for the next, and so on: $n!$ orders
$n \times (n - 1) \times \cdots$ for k places, but each set of k appears $k!$ times
${}_nC_k = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}$ counts the sets of k

chain.cause: Choosing k to include is choosing $n - k$ to leave out

ideas: A factorial $n! = n \times (n - 1) \times \cdots \times 2 \times 1$ counts the orders of n different items; $0! = 1$.
A combination ${}_nC_k = \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}$ counts the ways to choose k of n items when order does not matter.
Ordered choices overcount: $10 \times 9 \times 8 = 720$ counts each set of 3 six times, so ${}_{10}C_3 = 120$.
On a calculator or in Bluebook, type ${}_{10}C_3$ as 10C3 or nCr(10, 3).

misconception.wrong: There are $4 \times 3 = 12$ teams of 2 from 4 people.
misconception.right: 12 counts ordered pairs, so Ana with Ben is counted twice. Divide by $2! = 2$: ${}_4C_2 = 6$.

summary: A factorial $n!$ multiplies n by each whole number below it and counts the orders of n items ($0! = 1$). A combination ${}_nC_k = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}$ counts the ways to choose k of n when order does not matter; it equals ${}_nC_{n-k}$.
